newsitem.title: USA: Texas doctor goes on trial for selling cancer drug.
newsitem.headline: Texas doctor goes on trial for selling cancer drug.

text.p: Defence attorneys on Tuesday said a Polish-born doctor distributed an unapproved cancer drug because he wanted to help desperately ill people.
But prosecutors said Stanislaw Burzynski violated court orders and defrauded insurance companies so he could make money off a drug that had not been properly researched.

Attorneys for both sides made their comments in opening arguments of a trial in which Burzynski, 54, faces a 75-count indictment for selling a drug he manufactured from peptides found in human blood and urine.
He began administering the drug to patients in the late 1970s, but did not have Food and Drug Administration approval for a clinical trial until a year ago.

Defence attorney John Ackerman told the 12-member jury that Burzynski's drug was the last, best hope for many cancer patients. "They come to him as their last hope. We all would want that last hope," he said.

Burzynski, who developed neoplaston while he was a professor at Houston's Baylor College of Medicine, felt that not administering the drug, even without FDA approval, would violate his physician's oath to "do no harm," Ackerman said.
He said Burzynski was born in 1943 under Nazi rule in Poland, then resisted the Communist government installed after World War II.

He came to the United States in 1970 because "he yearned to be free," but instead had run afoul of the Food and Drug Administration, the medical establishment, federal and state courts and insurance companies, Ackerman said.
